title: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
tagline: Carbonyl reactivity, nucleophilic addition, Tollens and Fehling tests, aldol and Cannizzaro reactions, and the acidity of carboxylic acids.

overview.intro: An aldehyde or a ketone contains the carbonyl group, C=O, in which oxygen is much more electronegative than carbon, so the carbon carries a partial positive charge and the oxygen a partial negative charge. That polarisation is the key to the whole of carbonyl chemistry: the carbon is attacked by nucleophiles, and the oxygen is attacked by electrophiles and protonated by acids. Aldehydes and ketones differ in what is attached to the carbonyl group, and that difference governs both their reactivity, since two alkyl groups shield the carbon and release electron density, and their oxidation behaviour, since an aldehyde has a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon that a ketone does not. The unit covers the preparation of aldehydes and ketones from alcohols, alkenes, alkynes, acid chlorides, carboxylate salts, nitriles and esters; the mechanism of nucleophilic addition with hydrogen cyanide, sodium bisulphite, Grignard reagents and ammonia derivatives; reduction to alcohols and to alkanes by the Clemmensen and Wolff-Kishner methods; the base-catalysed aldol, cross-aldol and Cannizzaro reactions; and the tests, Tollens, Fehling and iodoform, that separate aldehydes from ketones and aliphatic from aromatic aldehydes. It then treats the carboxylic acids, whose acidity is explained by resonance stabilisation of the carboxylate ion and modified by substituents, together with the formation of acid derivatives, decarboxylation, the Kolbe electrolytic reaction and the Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction.

learningOutcomes: Name aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids by the IUPAC system and describe the structure and polarity of the carbonyl and carboxyl groups.
Describe the preparation of aldehydes and ketones from alcohols, alkenes, alkynes, acid chlorides, carboxylate salts, nitriles and esters.
Explain the mechanism of nucleophilic addition and account for the order of reactivity of aldehydes and ketones.
Describe reactions with hydrogen cyanide, sodium bisulphite, Grignard reagents, alcohols and ammonia derivatives, and the reduction reactions that give alcohols or alkanes.
Distinguish aldehydes from ketones, and aliphatic from aromatic aldehydes, using Tollens, Fehling and iodoform tests.
Describe the aldol, cross-aldol, Cannizzaro and benzoin reactions and explain the role of the alpha hydrogen.
Explain the acidity of carboxylic acids, the effect of substituents, the formation of acid derivatives, decarboxylation, the Kolbe electrolytic reaction and the Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction.

learn.title: Structure, nomenclature and preparation of aldehydes and ketones

blocks.text: In an aldehyde the carbonyl carbon is attached to at least one hydrogen, so the group is written -CHO and always sits at the end of a chain. In a ketone the carbonyl carbon is attached to two carbon atoms, so the group is written -CO- and sits inside the chain. The carbonyl carbon is sp2 hybridised and the group is planar, with bond angles of about 120 degrees, and the carbon-oxygen double bond consists of one sigma bond and one pi bond. Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the pi electrons are drawn towards oxygen, which gives the carbon a partial positive charge and makes it the electrophilic centre. In the IUPAC system aldehydes take the suffix -al, as in ethanal and benzaldehyde, and ketones take the suffix -one, as in propanone, with the chain numbered so that the carbonyl carbon receives the lowest possible locant.

items.meaning: The C=O group, planar and polar, whose electron-poor carbon is attacked by nucleophiles.
A compound in which the carbonyl carbon carries at least one hydrogen, giving the suffix -al.
A compound in which the carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbon atoms, giving the suffix -one.
A hydrogen attached to the carbon immediately next to a carbonyl group, acidic enough to be removed by base and responsible for aldol condensation.
The resonance-stabilised anion formed when a base removes an alpha hydrogen, with the negative charge shared between the alpha carbon and the carbonyl oxygen.

items: From alcohols: a primary alcohol is oxidised to an aldehyde and a secondary alcohol to a ketone, using acidified potassium dichromate or copper at high temperature.
From alkenes by ozonolysis: the double bond is cleaved and the two carbon atoms of the double bond become carbonyl carbons.
From alkynes by hydration: ethyne with dilute sulphuric acid and mercury(II) sulphate gives ethanal, while other alkynes give ketones.
From acid chlorides by Rosenmund reduction: hydrogen over palladium poisoned with barium sulphate converts an acid chloride into an aldehyde.
From acid chlorides with a dialkyl cadmium: the acyl chloride is converted into a ketone.
From the calcium salt of a carboxylic acid by dry distillation: calcium ethanoate gives propanone and calcium carbonate.
From nitriles by the Stephen reaction, using tin(II) chloride and hydrochloric acid, which gives an aldehyde.
From nitriles with a Grignard reagent followed by hydrolysis, which gives a ketone.
From esters by reduction with di-isobutylaluminium hydride at low temperature, which stops at the aldehyde.

items.text: Write the product of the ozonolysis of but-2-ene followed by reductive work-up.
items.note: Ozone cleaves the double bond and each carbon of the double bond becomes a carbonyl carbon. Since both carbons carry a methyl group, both products are ethanal, so two molecules of ethanal are obtained.

items.text: Why does the Rosenmund reduction stop at the aldehyde rather than going on to the alcohol?
items.note: The palladium catalyst is poisoned with barium sulphate, which reduces its activity so that it can reduce the acid chloride but cannot reduce the aldehyde further. Without the poisoning the aldehyde would be reduced to a primary alcohol.

blocks.text: The characteristic reaction of a carbonyl compound is nucleophilic addition. The nucleophile attacks the electron-poor carbonyl carbon, the pi bond breaks and both electrons move onto the oxygen, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate. That intermediate is then protonated, either by the solvent or during the work-up, to give the final addition product. Because the carbonyl carbon changes from trigonal planar to tetrahedral, the reaction can create a new chiral centre, and when the two faces of the carbonyl group are not equivalent a mixture of diastereomers results. The reactivity of a carbonyl compound towards addition depends on two factors: the size of the groups attached to the carbonyl carbon, which controls steric hindrance to the approaching nucleophile, and their electron-releasing power, which reduces the positive charge on the carbon. Methanal has only two hydrogens, so it is the least hindered and most reactive; each alkyl group that replaces a hydrogen makes the compound less reactive. Aromatic aldehydes and ketones are still less reactive because the ring conjugates with the carbonyl group and delocalises the positive charge.

blocks.caption: Table: Nucleophilic addition reactions of aldehydes and ketones
rows: Chain extension and synthesis of alpha-hydroxy acids
Bisulphite addition compound, a crystalline solid

Alcohol, primary from methanal, secondary from an aldehyde, tertiary from a ketone

blocks.text: The reaction with ammonia and its derivatives is the standard way of identifying a carbonyl compound, because each derivative is a crystalline solid with a sharp melting point. Hydroxylamine gives an oxime, hydrazine gives a hydrazone, phenylhydrazine gives a phenylhydrazone and semicarbazide gives a semicarbazone; in every case the nitrogen of the reagent attacks the carbonyl carbon, water is eliminated and a carbon-nitrogen double bond is formed. The reaction with alcohols gives a hemiacetal first, in which one alkoxy group and one hydroxyl group are attached to the same carbon, and then an acetal, in which both are alkoxy groups. Acetals are stable to base but are hydrolysed back to the carbonyl compound by aqueous acid, which is why they are used to protect a carbonyl group while reactions are carried out elsewhere in the molecule. With phosphorus pentachloride the carbonyl oxygen is replaced by two chlorine atoms, giving a gem-dichloride.

items: Nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl is faster for aldehydes than for ketones, and faster for aliphatic than for aromatic carbonyl compounds.
Hydrogen cyanide addition gives a cyanohydrin, which on hydrolysis gives an alpha-hydroxy acid.
Sodium bisulphite addition works for aldehydes, methyl ketones and unhindered cyclic ketones, but not for most other ketones.
Grignard addition followed by hydrolysis is the standard way of building a new carbon-carbon bond to a carbonyl carbon.
Formation of an oxime, hydrazone, phenylhydrazone or semicarbazone is used to characterise an unknown carbonyl compound.
Acetal formation protects a carbonyl group against attack by base or by nucleophiles.

items.text: Propanone is treated with hydrogen cyanide followed by hydrolysis of the nitrile. What is the final product?
items.note: The addition gives 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile. Hydrolysis of the nitrile group with dilute acid gives 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanoic acid, an alpha-hydroxy acid, so the sequence converts a ketone into a carboxylic acid with one more carbon.

items.text: Why does ethanal react with sodium bisulphite to give a crystalline solid while propanone reacts only slowly and butanone hardly at all?
items.note: The bisulphite addition is strongly sensitive to steric hindrance, because the bulky sulphite group must approach the carbonyl carbon. Ethanal has only a methyl group and a hydrogen, propanone has two methyl groups, and butanone has a methyl and an ethyl group, so the reactivity falls as the groups become larger.

blocks.text: Physical properties and uses: for comparable molar mass, boiling points follow carboxylic acids > alcohols > aldehydes/ketones > hydrocarbons/ethers, because aldehydes and ketones cannot form intermolecular hydrogen bonds with themselves (though they accept H-bonds from water) while alcohols and especially carboxylic acids (which dimerise) do. Formaldehyde (as formalin) is used in preservation and resins, acetaldehyde in manufacture of acetic acid and other chemicals, benzaldehyde in perfumery/flavouring, and acetone as an important solvent and in synthesis.

learn.title: Oxidation, reduction and the tests that distinguish carbonyl compounds

blocks.text: Aldehydes are readily oxidised to carboxylic acids because the carbonyl carbon still carries a hydrogen, while ketones resist oxidation because their carbonyl carbon carries no hydrogen and further oxidation would require breaking a carbon-carbon bond. This difference is the basis of the standard tests. Tollens reagent is ammoniacal silver nitrate: the aldehyde reduces the silver ion to metallic silver, which deposits as a mirror on the walls of a clean test tube, while the aldehyde is oxidised to the corresponding carboxylate. Fehling's solution is an alkaline solution of copper(II) tartrate: an aliphatic aldehyde reduces the blue copper(II) complex to a red precipitate of copper(I) oxide. Aromatic aldehydes such as benzaldehyde reduce Tollens reagent but not Fehling's solution, which is how an aromatic aldehyde is distinguished from an aliphatic one. The iodoform test uses iodine and sodium hydroxide and gives a yellow precipitate of triiodomethane with ethanal, with methyl ketones such as propanone, and with alcohols that contain the CH3CH(OH) group; benzaldehyde gives no precipitate.

Reduction of a carbonyl compound can stop at the alcohol or go all the way to the alkane. Lithium aluminium hydride and sodium borohydride reduce aldehydes and ketones to alcohols, and catalytic hydrogenation does the same. Complete reduction to the hydrocarbon requires the Clemmensen or the Wolff-Kishner method. Clemmensen reduction uses zinc amalgam and concentrated hydrochloric acid, and it works well for compounds that survive acid. Wolff-Kishner reduction uses hydrazine and potassium hydroxide in a high-boiling glycol solvent, and it works well for compounds that are sensitive to acid. Reduction with red phosphorus and concentrated hydriodic acid is a third route to the same result. The choice between Clemmensen and Wolff-Kishner is therefore made by looking at which functional groups elsewhere in the molecule would be damaged by acid or by base.

blocks.caption: Table: Tests that distinguish aldehydes and ketones

items: Benzaldehyde reduces Tollens reagent but not Fehling's solution, which distinguishes an aromatic from an aliphatic aldehyde.
Methanal and ethanal can be distinguished by the iodoform test, which is positive only for ethanal.
Acetone and benzaldehyde are distinguished by the iodoform test, positive for acetone, and by Tollens reagent, positive for benzaldehyde.
Formic acid reduces Tollens reagent because it contains a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon, although it is a carboxylic acid.
Clemmensen reduction suits acid-stable compounds, and Wolff-Kishner reduction suits base-stable compounds.

items.text: A compound of formula C3H6O gives a yellow precipitate with iodine and sodium hydroxide but does not reduce Fehling's solution. Identify it.
items.note: The positive iodoform test indicates a CH3CO group, and the failure to reduce Fehling's solution indicates a ketone rather than an aldehyde. The compound is propanone, CH3COCH3, which has the required formula and both properties.

items.text: Why is Tollens reagent prepared fresh and used immediately?
items.note: Ammoniacal silver nitrate slowly decomposes on standing, depositing silver and forming the explosive silver nitride, so it is prepared fresh and used at once. The test tube must also be very clean, otherwise the silver deposits as a black powder instead of a mirror.

learn.title: The alpha hydrogen, aldol and Cannizzaro reactions, and benzaldehyde

blocks.text: A hydrogen attached to the carbon next to a carbonyl group is weakly acidic, because the anion formed when it is removed is stabilised by resonance with the carbonyl group. This anion, the enolate, has the negative charge shared between the alpha carbon and the carbonyl oxygen, so it is stable enough for base to remove the proton. The enolate can then attack the carbonyl carbon of another molecule, which is the first step of the aldol condensation. With dilute sodium hydroxide, two molecules of an aldehyde or ketone that has alpha hydrogens combine to give a beta-hydroxy carbonyl compound, the aldol, and on heating the aldol loses water to give an alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl compound. With two different carbonyl compounds the reaction is a cross-aldol, and because each compound can act as either the nucleophile or the electrophile, a mixture of four products is usually obtained.

When a carbonyl compound has no alpha hydrogen, the aldol route is impossible, and in concentrated alkali a different reaction takes place. Two molecules of the aldehyde react with each other, one is oxidised to the carboxylate ion and the other is reduced to the alcohol, and the same carbon that loses oxygen gains hydrogen: this is the Cannizzaro reaction. Methanal gives methanol and sodium formate, and benzaldehyde gives benzyl alcohol and sodium benzoate. The reaction is a disproportionation, and it requires a concentrated base because the hydroxide must both add to the carbonyl and remove a hydride from the intermediate. Benzaldehyde shows several other characteristic reactions because it has no alpha hydrogen and an activated ring: benzoin condensation with alcoholic potassium cyanide gives benzoin, the Perkin reaction with acetic anhydride and sodium acetate gives cinnamic acid, and electrophilic substitution on the ring gives the meta-substituted products expected for a carbonyl substituent.

items: Aldol condensation: two molecules with alpha hydrogen, dilute sodium hydroxide, beta-hydroxy carbonyl, then dehydration on heating.
Cross-aldol: two different carbonyl compounds, giving a mixture of products because either can supply the enolate.
Cannizzaro reaction: an aldehyde with no alpha hydrogen and concentrated sodium hydroxide, giving an alcohol and a carboxylate.
Benzoin condensation: benzaldehyde with alcoholic potassium cyanide gives benzoin, C6H5CH(OH)COC6H5.
Perkin reaction: benzaldehyde with acetic anhydride and sodium acetate gives cinnamic acid, C6H5CH=CHCOOH.
Benzaldehyde is prepared from toluene by oxidation with chromyl chloride, the Etard reaction, or by the hydrolysis of benzylidene chloride.
Benzaldehyde with concentrated sodium hydroxide gives benzyl alcohol and sodium benzoate, its Cannizzaro reaction.
Benzaldehyde with hydrogen cyanide gives mandelonitrile, and with sodium bisulphite gives the bisulphite addition compound.
Benzaldehyde with ammonia derivatives gives the corresponding oxime, hydrazone or phenylhydrazone, and with phosphorus pentachloride gives benzylidene chloride.
Electrophilic substitution of benzaldehyde gives mainly the meta product, because the carbonyl group withdraws electron density.

items.text: Why does ethanal undergo aldol condensation but benzaldehyde undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction?
items.note: Ethanal has three alpha hydrogens on its methyl group, so a base can form an enolate and the aldol condensation can proceed. Benzaldehyde has no alpha hydrogen, because the carbon next to the carbonyl group is part of the ring and carries no hydrogen, so no enolate can form and the Cannizzaro disproportionation takes over in concentrated alkali.

items.text: Propanone is treated with dilute sodium hydroxide and the product is heated. What is the final product?
items.note: Two molecules of propanone combine to give the aldol 4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one, and heating dehydrates it to 4-methylpent-3-en-2-one, an alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone. The dehydration is favoured because the resulting double bond is conjugated with the carbonyl group.

learn.title: Carboxylic acids: acidity, preparation and reactions

blocks.text: A carboxylic acid contains the carboxyl group, -COOH, in which a carbonyl group and a hydroxyl group are attached to the same carbon. The group is planar and the two oxygens are not equivalent: the carbonyl oxygen is doubly bonded and the hydroxyl oxygen singly bonded. Carboxylic acids are far more acidic than alcohols and phenols because the carboxylate ion formed on losing a proton is stabilised by resonance, with the negative charge shared equally between the two oxygen atoms. Since both oxygens are identical in the resonance hybrid, the ion is unusually stable and the acid is correspondingly strong, with acetic acid having a pKa of about 4.76 compared with about 10 for phenol and about 16 for ethanol. Carboxylic acids therefore liberate carbon dioxide from sodium bicarbonate, which neither alcohols nor phenols do.

The acidity of a carboxylic acid is modified by substituents. An electron-withdrawing group stabilises the carboxylate ion by dispersing the negative charge and increases the acidity, so trichloroacetic acid is a much stronger acid than acetic acid, and the effect grows with the number of chlorine atoms and with their proximity to the carboxyl group. An electron-releasing alkyl group has the opposite effect, so propanoic acid is slightly weaker than acetic acid. Benzoic acid is stronger than acetic acid because the ring withdraws electron density inductively, and substituents on the ring act in the expected way, with a nitro group increasing acidity and a methyl or methoxy group decreasing it. An ortho substituent often produces an unexpectedly large effect, the ortho effect, which makes almost any ortho-substituted benzoic acid stronger than benzoic acid itself, largely because of steric inhibition of resonance and of solvation.

items: Preparation from alcohols and aldehydes by oxidation with acidified potassium dichromate or potassium permanganate.
Preparation from nitriles by hydrolysis with dilute acid or alkali, which gives the acid with the same number of carbons.
Preparation from a Grignard reagent and carbon dioxide, followed by acidification, which gives an acid with one more carbon.
With active metals, acids give the carboxylate salt and hydrogen.
With alkalies, carbonates and bicarbonates, acids give the carboxylate salt, and with carbonates and bicarbonates carbon dioxide is also evolved.
With alcohols in the presence of an acid catalyst, acids give esters, the reaction being reversible.
With phosphorus pentachloride, thionyl chloride or phosphorus trichloride, acids give acid chlorides.
Heating with phosphorus pentoxide gives the acid anhydride, and heating the ammonium salt gives the amide.
Decarboxylation: the sodium salt heated with soda lime gives an alkane with one carbon less.
Kolbe electrolytic reaction: electrolysis of the potassium salt gives an alkane with twice the number of carbons and carbon dioxide at the anode.
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction: bromine with a little red phosphorus gives the alpha-bromo acid.
Nitration and sulphonation of benzoic acid give the meta products, because the carboxyl group is meta-directing.

items.text: Why does formic acid reduce Tollens reagent while acetic acid does not?
items.note: Formic acid has a hydrogen on its carbonyl carbon, so it can be oxidised to carbon dioxide and water and can reduce silver ions to silver. Acetic acid has a methyl group on the carbonyl carbon instead of a hydrogen, so it cannot be oxidised in this way and gives no silver mirror.

items.text: Arrange acetic acid, chloroacetic acid, dichloroacetic acid and trichloroacetic acid in order of increasing acidity.
items.note: The order is acetic, then chloroacetic, then dichloroacetic, then trichloroacetic acid. Each chlorine atom withdraws electron density inductively, stabilising the carboxylate ion more, so the acidity increases with the number of chlorine atoms on the alpha carbon.

blocks.text: Carboxylic acids may be monocarboxylic (one –COOH group, e.g. formic acid, acetic acid, benzoic acid) or dicarboxylic/polycarboxylic (two or more –COOH groups, e.g. oxalic acid, malonic acid, succinic acid, phthalic acid). Common uses include acetic acid in vinegar and as a chemical reagent/solvent, formic acid in textile/leather processing and as a preservative, benzoic acid and its salts as food preservatives, and oxalic acid in cleaning/bleaching applications.

keyPoints: The carbonyl group is planar and polar, with a partial positive charge on carbon that makes it the site of nucleophilic attack.
Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition because they are less hindered and less electron-rich.
The characteristic reaction of the carbonyl group is nucleophilic addition through a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate.
Tollens reagent gives a silver mirror with aldehydes, and Fehling's solution gives red copper(I) oxide with aliphatic but not aromatic aldehydes.
The iodoform test is positive for ethanal and for methyl ketones, and negative for benzaldehyde.
Clemmensen reduction uses zinc amalgam and hydrochloric acid, and Wolff-Kishner reduction uses hydrazine and potassium hydroxide, to convert carbonyl groups into methylene groups.
An alpha hydrogen is acidic because the enolate ion is stabilised by resonance, and it is required for aldol condensation.
An aldehyde with no alpha hydrogen undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction with concentrated alkali, giving an alcohol and a carboxylate.
The carboxylate ion is stabilised by resonance over two equivalent oxygen atoms, which makes carboxylic acids far stronger acids than alcohols or phenols.

Electron-withdrawing substituents increase the acidity of a carboxylic acid and electron-releasing substituents decrease it, and the acid derivatives react in the order acid chloride > anhydride > ester > amide.

vocabulary.meaning: The C=O group, planar and polar, which undergoes nucleophilic addition.
Addition of a nucleophile to a carbonyl carbon, giving a tetrahedral intermediate that is then protonated.
The product of addition of hydrogen cyanide to a carbonyl compound, containing both a hydroxyl and a nitrile group on the same carbon.
The product formed when hydroxylamine reacts with a carbonyl compound, containing a C=N-OH group.
A compound in which two alkoxy groups are attached to the same carbon, formed from an aldehyde or ketone and two molecules of alcohol, and used to protect the carbonyl group.
A hydrogen on the carbon adjacent to a carbonyl group, removable by base to give a resonance-stabilised enolate.
Base-catalysed combination of two carbonyl molecules with alpha hydrogens to give a beta-hydroxy carbonyl compound, which may then dehydrate.
Disproportionation of an aldehyde with no alpha hydrogen in concentrated alkali into an alcohol and a carboxylate.
Ammoniacal silver nitrate, reduced to a silver mirror by aldehydes and by formic acid.
Alkaline copper(II) tartrate, reduced to red copper(I) oxide by aliphatic aldehydes but not by aromatic aldehydes or ketones.
Reduction of a carbonyl group to a methylene group using zinc amalgam and concentrated hydrochloric acid.
Reduction of a carbonyl group to a methylene group using hydrazine and potassium hydroxide in a glycol solvent.
The -COOH group, whose resonance-stabilised conjugate base makes carboxylic acids far more acidic than alcohols.
Loss of carbon dioxide from a carboxylic acid or its salt, as when the sodium salt with soda lime gives an alkane with one carbon less.
Bromination at the alpha carbon of a carboxylic acid using bromine and a little red phosphorus.

figures.caption: Figure: Mechanism of nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl group
figures.description: A carbonyl compound is drawn with the polarised C=O bond and a nucleophile approaching the carbon. Curved arrows show the nucleophile attacking the carbon while the pi electrons move onto the oxygen, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate with a negative charge on oxygen. A final step shows protonation of that oxygen to give the addition product.
labels: carbonyl carbon with partial positive charge
carbonyl oxygen with partial negative charge
curved arrow from nucleophile to carbon

figures.caption: Figure: Resonance stabilisation of the carboxylate ion
figures.description: A carboxylic acid is shown losing its proton to give the carboxylate ion. Two equivalent resonance structures are drawn, in which the negative charge alternates between the two oxygen atoms and the carbon-oxygen bond order is intermediate between single and double in each. The equivalence of the two oxygens explains the stability of the ion.
labels: negative charge on the other oxygen
equal carbon-oxygen bond lengths in the hybrid

figures.caption: Figure: Energy profile showing why aldehydes are more reactive than ketones
figures.description: Two reaction coordinate curves are drawn for the addition of a nucleophile, one for an aldehyde and one for a ketone. The ketone curve has a higher activation energy and a higher-energy product, because the two alkyl groups hinder the approach of the nucleophile and release electron density onto the carbonyl carbon. The aldehyde therefore reacts faster and more completely.
labels: lower activation energy for the aldehyde
higher activation energy for the ketone
steric hindrance from two alkyl groups

questions.prompt: Which compound is most reactive towards nucleophilic addition?
questions.answer: Methanal
questions.explanation: Methanal has two hydrogen atoms on the carbonyl carbon, so there is almost no steric hindrance and no electron-releasing alkyl group to reduce the positive charge on that carbon. Each alkyl group added makes the carbonyl carbon less accessible and less electrophilic, so reactivity falls from methanal through ethanal and propanone to aromatic ketones.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing propanone because it is the most familiar ketone.

questions.prompt: Tollens reagent is:
options: a solution of iodine in sodium hydroxide
questions.answer: ammoniacal silver nitrate
questions.explanation: Tollens reagent is silver nitrate dissolved in excess ammonia, which gives the soluble diamminesilver(I) ion. An aldehyde reduces it to metallic silver, which deposits as a mirror, while a ketone does not react.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing Tollens reagent with Fehling's solution, which is the copper tartrate reagent.

questions.prompt: Which compound does not give a yellow precipitate with iodine and sodium hydroxide?
questions.answer: Benzaldehyde
questions.explanation: The iodoform test is positive for a CH3CO group or a CH3CH(OH) group. Ethanal and propanone contain the methyl ketone arrangement, and ethanol is oxidised to ethanal under the conditions, so all three give a yellow precipitate of triiodomethane. Benzaldehyde has no methyl group next to the carbonyl carbon, so it gives no precipitate.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming that any aldehyde gives the iodoform test.

questions.prompt: The Cannizzaro reaction is given by an aldehyde that:
options: has at least one alpha hydrogen
questions.answer: has no alpha hydrogen
questions.explanation: An aldehyde with an alpha hydrogen undergoes aldol condensation in alkali instead. When no alpha hydrogen is available, as in methanal and benzaldehyde, concentrated alkali brings about disproportionation into the corresponding alcohol and carboxylate, which is the Cannizzaro reaction.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking that all aldehydes undergo the Cannizzaro reaction in alkali.

questions.prompt: The Clemmensen reduction of a ketone uses:
options: zinc amalgam and concentrated hydrochloric acid
hydrogen over a poisoned palladium catalyst
questions.answer: zinc amalgam and concentrated hydrochloric acid
questions.explanation: The Clemmensen reduction converts a carbonyl group into a methylene group using zinc amalgam in concentrated hydrochloric acid. Hydrazine with potassium hydroxide is the Wolff-Kishner reduction, sodium borohydride stops at the alcohol, and poisoned palladium is used for the Rosenmund reduction of an acid chloride.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing the Clemmensen reagents with those of the Wolff-Kishner reduction.

questions.prompt: Benzaldehyde reduces Tollens reagent but not Fehling's solution. This observation is used to distinguish:
options: a carboxylic acid from a phenol
an aromatic aldehyde from an aliphatic aldehyde
a primary alcohol from a secondary alcohol
questions.answer: an aromatic aldehyde from an aliphatic aldehyde
questions.explanation: Both aliphatic and aromatic aldehydes reduce Tollens reagent, but only aliphatic aldehydes reduce Fehling's solution. A compound that gives a silver mirror but no red copper(I) oxide precipitate is therefore an aromatic aldehyde such as benzaldehyde.
questions.commonMistake: Using this pair of tests to distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone, when Tollens alone does that.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest acid?
questions.answer: Trichloroacetic acid
questions.explanation: Each chlorine atom withdraws electron density inductively from the carboxyl group, which stabilises the carboxylate ion by dispersing its negative charge. Acidity therefore increases with the number of chlorine atoms, making trichloroacetic acid the strongest of the four.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming that the acid with the most hydrogen atoms available is the strongest.

questions.prompt: Benzoyl chloride is converted into benzaldehyde by the Rosenmund reduction, which uses:
options: lithium aluminium hydride in dry ether
hydrogen over palladium poisoned with barium sulphate
questions.answer: hydrogen over palladium poisoned with barium sulphate
questions.explanation: Rosenmund reduction hydrogenates an acid chloride to an aldehyde over palladium that has been deliberately poisoned with barium sulphate, which stops the reduction at the aldehyde stage. Lithium aluminium hydride would reduce the acid chloride all the way to a primary alcohol.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing lithium aluminium hydride, which does not stop at the aldehyde.

questions.prompt: Aldehydes and ketones react with hydroxylamine to form an ______.
questions.answer: oxime
questions.explanation: The nitrogen of hydroxylamine attacks the carbonyl carbon, water is eliminated and a carbon-nitrogen double bond is formed, giving an oxime with the group C=N-OH. Oximes are crystalline solids and are used to identify carbonyl compounds.
questions.commonMistake: Writing hydrazone, which is the product with hydrazine.

questions.prompt: In the Rosenmund reduction the hydrogenation catalyst is palladium supported on barium sulphate, which acts as a ______.
questions.answer: poison
questions.explanation: Barium sulphate reduces the activity of the palladium catalyst so that it can reduce the acid chloride but cannot reduce the aldehyde further to an alcohol. A deliberately deactivated catalyst of this kind is called a poisoned catalyst.
questions.commonMistake: Calling barium sulphate a promoter, which would imply that it increases activity.

questions.prompt: Carboxylic acids react with sodium bicarbonate to liberate ______ gas.
questions.answer: carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: A carboxylic acid is stronger than carbonic acid, so it displaces carbon dioxide from a bicarbonate. The observation of effervescence distinguishes a carboxylic acid from a phenol, which is too weakly acidic to react in this way.
questions.commonMistake: Writing hydrogen, which is liberated by reaction with sodium metal rather than with bicarbonate.

questions.prompt: Explain why aldehydes are more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition.
questions.answer: An aldehyde has at least one hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon, while a ketone has two alkyl groups. The alkyl groups are larger than hydrogen, so they hinder the approach of the nucleophile to the carbonyl carbon, and they also release electron density inductively, which reduces the positive charge on that carbon. Both effects lower the reactivity of a ketone relative to an aldehyde, so aldehydes undergo nucleophilic addition faster.
questions.explanation: The two effects act together, one steric and one electronic, which is why the reactivity order is methanal, then other aldehydes, then ketones, then aromatic ketones.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only the steric reason without mentioning the electron-releasing effect of the alkyl groups.

questions.prompt: Describe one chemical test that distinguishes ethanal from propanone, stating the observation for each.
questions.answer: Tollens reagent distinguishes them. Ethanal is an aldehyde, so it reduces ammoniacal silver nitrate to metallic silver and deposits a silver mirror on the walls of the tube. Propanone is a ketone and has no hydrogen on its carbonyl carbon, so it cannot be oxidised in this way and gives no silver mirror. The iodoform test cannot be used here, because ethanal and propanone both contain a CH3CO group and both give a yellow precipitate.
questions.explanation: The distinction rests on the oxidation of the aldehyde, which Tollens reagent carries out, while both compounds share the methyl ketone arrangement that the iodoform test detects.
questions.commonMistake: Claiming that the iodoform test distinguishes ethanal from propanone, when both are positive.

questions.prompt: Why does benzaldehyde not undergo aldol condensation?
questions.answer: Aldol condensation requires an alpha hydrogen, which is removed by base to form an enolate that then attacks another carbonyl group. In benzaldehyde the carbon adjacent to the carbonyl group is a ring carbon that already carries three bonds and no hydrogen, so no alpha hydrogen is available and no enolate can form. Benzaldehyde therefore undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction in concentrated alkali instead.
questions.explanation: The absence of the alpha hydrogen blocks the first step of the aldol route, and the Cannizzaro disproportionation becomes the available pathway.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that benzaldehyde is too stable or too aromatic to react, rather than identifying the missing alpha hydrogen.

questions.prompt: Arrange acetic acid, benzoic acid and trichloroacetic acid in order of increasing acidity, giving a reason for the order.
questions.answer: The order of increasing acidity is acetic acid, then benzoic acid, then trichloroacetic acid. Acidity depends on the stability of the carboxylate ion, and the three chlorine atoms of trichloroacetic acid withdraw electron density strongly by their inductive effect, which disperses the negative charge and stabilises the ion most. The benzene ring of benzoic acid also withdraws electron density relative to the methyl group of acetic acid, so benzoic acid is stronger than acetic acid but much weaker than trichloroacetic acid.
questions.explanation: The comparison is entirely about how well each substituent stabilises the negative charge of the conjugate base, with electron withdrawal increasing acidity and electron release decreasing it.
questions.commonMistake: Ordering by molar mass or by the number of carbon atoms instead of by substituent effects.

questions.prompt: Describe the mechanism of nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl group, using the reaction of ethanal with hydrogen cyanide as the example.
questions.answer: The carbonyl group is polar, with a partial positive charge on carbon and a partial negative charge on oxygen. The cyanide ion, which is a strong nucleophile, attacks the carbonyl carbon, and the pi electrons of the carbon-oxygen double bond move onto the oxygen, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate in which the carbon carries a negative charge on oxygen and a new carbon-carbon bond to the cyanide. This intermediate is then protonated, either by water or by the hydrogen cyanide itself, to give the cyanohydrin, 2-hydroxypropanenitrile. The overall change is addition across the carbon-oxygen double bond with no leaving group, which is why the reaction is an addition rather than a substitution.
questions.explanation: The key feature is that the pi bond opens and both fragments are retained, giving a tetrahedral product, and the protonation step is what converts the intermediate anion into a neutral cyanohydrin.
questions.commonMistake: Writing the mechanism as a substitution with cyanide replacing the oxygen.

questions.prompt: Describe three characteristic reactions of benzaldehyde that depend on the absence of an alpha hydrogen, giving the product in each case.
questions.answer: First, benzaldehyde undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction with concentrated sodium hydroxide, in which two molecules disproportionate so that one is oxidised to sodium benzoate and the other is reduced to benzyl alcohol. Second, it undergoes the benzoin condensation when heated with alcoholic potassium cyanide, in which two molecules combine to give benzoin, C6H5CH(OH)COC6H5. Third, it undergoes the Perkin reaction when heated with acetic anhydride and sodium acetate, giving cinnamic acid, C6H5CH=CHCOOH. In each case the absence of an alpha hydrogen prevents the aldol route and allows these alternative reactions of the carbonyl group to take place.
questions.explanation: The three reactions are united by the same structural feature, so grouping them under the missing alpha hydrogen is both accurate and easier to recall than three unconnected equations.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the aldol condensation of benzaldehyde, which cannot occur for want of an alpha hydrogen.

questions.prompt: Describe the formation of the four main carboxylic acid derivatives from a carboxylic acid, and arrange them in order of reactivity towards nucleophilic acyl substitution.
questions.answer: A carboxylic acid with phosphorus pentachloride, thionyl chloride or phosphorus trichloride gives the acid chloride. Heating the acid with phosphorus pentoxide gives the acid anhydride. Heating the acid with an alcohol in the presence of a small amount of acid catalyst gives the ester. Heating the ammonium salt of the acid gives the amide. The order of reactivity towards nucleophilic acyl substitution is acid chloride, then acid anhydride, then ester, then amide. The order follows the ability of the group attached to the carbonyl to donate electron density and to leave: chloride donates least and leaves best, while the nitrogen of an amide donates its lone pair strongly and is a poor leaving group.
questions.explanation: The same two factors, electron donation into the carbonyl and leaving-group ability, explain the whole reactivity series, so the order is not arbitrary.
questions.commonMistake: Placing the amide above the ester, when the strong delocalisation of the nitrogen lone pair makes the amide the least reactive.

questions.prompt: Convert propan-1-ol into propan-2-one, naming each reagent and intermediate.
questions.answer: Propan-1-ol is first dehydrated by heating with concentrated sulphuric acid at about 443 K, which gives propene. Propene is then hydrated with steam over phosphoric acid, and Markovnikov addition places the hydroxyl group on the middle carbon, giving propan-2-ol. Propan-2-ol is oxidised with acidified potassium dichromate to propanone. The three steps are therefore propan-1-ol to propene to propan-2-ol to propanone, and the dehydration-hydration pair is what moves the hydroxyl group from the end of the chain to the middle; direct oxidation of propan-1-ol would give only propanal or propanoic acid.
questions.explanation: The direct oxidation of propan-1-ol gives propanal or propanoic acid, never a ketone, so the hydroxyl group must be moved to the middle carbon before oxidation can produce propanone.
questions.commonMistake: Oxidising propan-1-ol directly and expecting propanone, which would require the hydroxyl group to move.

questions.prompt: Give one chemical test to distinguish formaldehyde from ethanal, and one to distinguish an aliphatic aldehyde from an aromatic aldehyde, stating the observations.
questions.answer: Formaldehyde and ethanal are distinguished by the iodoform test: ethanal gives a yellow precipitate of triiodomethane with iodine and sodium hydroxide, while formaldehyde gives no precipitate because it has no methyl group next to the carbonyl carbon. An aliphatic aldehyde and an aromatic aldehyde are distinguished by Fehling's solution: the aliphatic aldehyde gives a red precipitate of copper(I) oxide, while the aromatic aldehyde gives no precipitate, although both reduce Tollens reagent to a silver mirror.
questions.explanation: The iodoform test detects the CH3CO arrangement, which ethanal has and formaldehyde does not, and Fehling's solution detects the ease of oxidation that aromatic aldehydes lack.
questions.commonMistake: Using Tollens reagent to separate the two aldehydes, since both give a silver mirror.

questions.prompt: 10.6 g of benzaldehyde is treated with concentrated sodium hydroxide until the Cannizzaro reaction is complete. Calculate the mass of benzyl alcohol and the mass of sodium benzoate formed. Molar masses: benzaldehyde 106, benzyl alcohol 108, sodium benzoate 144 g mol^-1.
questions.answer: Moles of benzaldehyde = 10.6 / 106 = 0.100 mol. The Cannizzaro reaction consumes two molecules of aldehyde to give one molecule of alcohol and one of carboxylate, so 0.100 mol of benzaldehyde gives 0.050 mol of benzyl alcohol and 0.050 mol of sodium benzoate. The mass of benzyl alcohol is 0.050 x 108 = 5.4 g, and the mass of sodium benzoate is 0.050 x 144 = 7.2 g. The total mass, 12.6 g, equals the mass of aldehyde plus the sodium hydroxide that has been incorporated.
questions.explanation: The two-to-one stoichiometry of the disproportionation is the step most often missed, and it follows from one molecule being oxidised while the other is reduced.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming a one-to-one stoichiometry and obtaining 10.8 g and 14.4 g.

questions.prompt: Formic acid reduces Tollens reagent and decarboxylates on heating with concentrated sulphuric acid, while acetic acid does neither. Explain both differences in terms of structure.
questions.answer: Formic acid has a hydrogen atom on its carbonyl carbon, so it can be oxidised to carbon dioxide and water, and that oxidation allows it to reduce silver ions to metallic silver. Acetic acid has a methyl group in place of that hydrogen, so it cannot be oxidised in the same way and gives no silver mirror. Formic acid also decomposes on heating with concentrated sulphuric acid to give carbon monoxide and water, because it is the only carboxylic acid with a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon that can be lost together with the hydroxyl group. Acetic acid has no such hydrogen, so it does not decompose in this way.
questions.explanation: Both differences come from the same structural feature, the hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon, which formic acid has and every other carboxylic acid lacks.
questions.commonMistake: Explaining the reducing behaviour by the acidic hydrogen of the carboxyl group, which every carboxylic acid has.
